_readme: U4 Future time, all 8 points. Sequence indices are drawn from this agent's private band 1300-1399 and are re-seated topologically by the post-merge renumbering pass.
gr_future_perfect is the deliberate listing/order mismatch whitelisted in DESIGN.md 4.1: it is listed in U4 but depends on the perfect, which is taught in U6.
Every point is a member of cs_future_selection; gr_future_choice is the one choice point and owns the contrast board gb_future_selection.
No vocabulary is authored in this block.

points.title: Saying what I expect to happen, and deciding something out loud as I speak

point_json.grammar_name: will for prediction, instant decision, offer, promise and refusal

teach.can_do: I can say what I expect to happen, and I can decide something out loud while I am speaking.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the first way of pointing forward that English gives you, it costs one unchanging word, and an essay wants it for every prediction you make.
teach.meaning: Will puts something in the part of time that has not arrived yet, and it does so out of your own head rather than out of anything standing in front of you. Reach for it when you believe something is ahead, when you make up your mind at the moment of speaking, when you offer to do something, and when you promise. Nothing has been arranged and nothing has been set up. The future here is your judgement, and it is being made now.

form.pattern: will + the plain verb, with nothing added to it
notes: the plain verb means no -s, no -ed and no to in front of it
in speech and in a friendly message it shrinks to 'll after a pronoun; an essay writes will in full
it never changes for he, she or it, which makes it the easiest thing in this unit to build
form.negative: will not, or won't in speech: The depot won't reopen before April.
form.question: Will + person + the plain verb: Will you send me the figures?

marks.label: you judge, or you decide, here

spec.caption: Will jumps straight from your head now to the thing itself. There is no preparation on the way.

worked_example.sentence: Fares on the Ashfield line will rise again in the spring.
worked_example.why_this_form: This is a judgement inside the speaker's head. No fare has been printed and no announcement has been made; the speaker simply expects it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Fares are rising would say the increase is already fixed and dated by the company, which is a far stronger claim than this speaker can make.

notice_set.sentence: I'll carry those boxes up for you.
notice_set.question: Had the speaker planned this before the conversation started?
notice_set.why: The offer is invented at the moment of speaking, which is exactly the job this word is doing here.

notice_set.sentence: The new footbridge at Sandmouth will open in the autumn.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving you something they expect, or something they have arranged themselves?
notice_set.why: The speaker is reporting what they believe is ahead. Nothing here says the plan is theirs.

notice_set.sentence: Kwame won't answer his phone while he is driving.
notice_set.question: Is this about a refusal, or about something happening at this moment?
notice_set.why: Won't very often carries a refusal: he will not do it, and that is his own choice.

notice_set.sentence: Levels in the Verdon will drop once the sluice gates open.
notice_set.question: Have the levels dropped yet?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence sits in a part of time nobody has reached, so nothing in it has happened.

notice_set.sentence: I'll ask Rehana to send the file across.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already know that Rehana is going to send it?
notice_set.why: The speaker is committing to their own next move. What Rehana then does is left wide open.

teach.rule_line: If the future is coming out of your own head right now, use will.
teach.false_rule: That will is simply how English says the future. English points forward in four ways, and will is only the one that comes out of your own head.

errors.wrong: The council will to publish the figures in June.
errors.right: The council will publish the figures in June.
errors.why_it_happens: Learners meet to in front of most verbs that follow another verb, so the hand supplies it out of habit. Nothing sounds broken on a re-read, so it survives all the way to the page.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: She will goes to the site meeting instead of me.
errors.right: She will go to the site meeting instead of me.
errors.why_it_happens: The ending that belongs on a verb after she has been drilled so hard that it fires anyway, even though will has already taken over the job of saying who and when.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on goes.

errors.wrong: Driverless buses will replace every driver in the country within ten years.
errors.right: Driverless buses will probably replace many drivers within ten years.
errors.why_it_happens: Will feels like a neutral way of pointing forward, so a guess gets attached to it as confidently as a certainty, and the reader hears a promise the writer has no way of keeping.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: probably.

errors.wrong: Careful with that tray, you will drop it.
errors.right: Careful with that tray, you're going to drop it.
errors.why_it_happens: Will is the first future most learners are handed, so it becomes the one that arrives first, even when the reason for saying it is wobbling in front of both people.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will drop becomes are going to drop.

pays_in.note: Every prediction paragraph is built on it, usually with a softening word beside it.
pays_in.model: Rising insurance costs will probably push some households away from the coast altogether.

pays_in.note: Offers, promises and decisions made mid-sentence all live here.
pays_in.model: I'll probably stay in this job another year, then have a look around.

pays_in.note: Announcements about what happens next are made of it.
pays_in.model: The replacement coach will leave from the far end of the car park.

used_in.quote: The examiner asks what the candidate thinks is ahead, and the answer starts with this word almost every time.
Arguing that a shorter week would spread is a prediction, and a prediction needs this and a softener.

payload.sentence: I'll take the early shift on Thursday if nobody else wants it.
payload.question: Was this settled before the conversation began?

feedback.why_key: The speaker is making up their mind while they talk. Nothing was agreed with anybody beforehand.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the speaker decided this while speaking.

payload.sentence: Rainfall across the Verdon catchment will fall by roughly a tenth this century.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a judgement about a stretch of time nobody has reached yet, so none of it has happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the event on a line before you read anything else.

payload.context: Rehana is answering a colleague who has just asked for a hand in the loading bay.
payload.sentence: I will to move the pallets before lunch.
reasons: there is one word too many after will
the speaker has not decided anything yet
the pallets have already been moved
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Will already carries the job of pointing forward, so the verb behind it stays plain and bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the verb behind will down to its plain shape.

payload.context: From a short note on the Brackenfield regeneration scheme.
payload.stem: If the funding holds, the market square ___ (reopen) before the winter.

feedback.why_key: The writer is predicting from what they know about the funding. Nothing has been arranged with anyone.
feedback.feed_forward: Put will in front and leave the verb completely plain.

payload.context: Two colleagues splitting up the jobs nobody has claimed.
payload.stem: Leave the invoices, I ___ (sort) them out this afternoon.

feedback.why_key: The speaker takes the job on at the moment of speaking, which is what this word is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the short form when you are speaking to somebody.

payload.given: Borrowing costs stand at four per cent. Most analysts expect a small cut in June.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying what is expected, and soften it so it is not read as a promise.

expected: will probably be cut in june

feedback.why_key: A prediction with nothing softening it reads as a guarantee, and no writer can guarantee what a committee does.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a softening word between will and the verb.

payload.context: A tutor answering a student on the way out of a seminar.

expected: i will send you the reading list tonight

feedback.why_key: Will sits straight after the person and the verb behind it stays bare, with the rest of the sentence following normally.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep will next to the person and the verb right behind it.

payload.audio_text: They'll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens.

expected: they'll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens
theyll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens
they will put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens

feedback.why_key: In speech the whole word shrinks onto the person in front of it, and one unstressed sound is all that is left of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small sound stuck to the person, not for a whole word.

items.decision_cue: will do every job in the country

payload.context: From a first draft of an essay about automation.
payload.sentence: Within twenty years, machines will do every job in the country.
reasons: a guess is being stated as a certainty
the sentence points at the wrong stretch of time
the verb behind will is built wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Every job is an absolute claim and nobody can stand behind it. The reader stops trusting the paragraph, not just the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Soften any prediction you could not defend if challenged.

payload.sentence: The board will to announce the outcome of the review on Friday morning.

feedback.why_key: Nothing else in the sentence is wrong. One extra word is doing all the damage, and it is the smallest one there.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the to that has crept in behind will.

payload.context: Two remarks about the same block of flats, made on different days.
sentences: That lift will break down again, I know that building.
That lift is going to break down, listen to the noise it is making.
meanings: The speaker is judging from experience they carry around in their head.
The speaker is pointing at something both people can notice this minute.

feedback.why_key: Both speakers expect the same breakdown. Only one of them can put a finger on the reason while they say it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the reason is in the room or in the speaker.

payload.prompt_text: A colleague has just asked you to cover a task you had not planned on doing. Answer them, take it on, and say when you can get to it.

feedback.why_key: You are agreeing to something at the moment of speaking, and that is the situation this word was made for.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide inside the sentence rather than reporting an old plan.

payload.prompt_text: Open your last essay on city centres and add one closing sentence predicting what happens if nothing is changed. Soften it so a reader could not call it a promise. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A closing prediction is what turns an argument into a position, and the softener is what keeps the position defensible.
feedback.feed_forward: Predict once, soften once, then stop.

points.title: Saying what I have already decided to do, and what the signs in front of me point to

point_json.grammar_name: be going to for intention and for evidence-based prediction

teach.can_do: I can say what I have already made up my mind to do, and what the signs around me are pointing to.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the future of ordinary speech, and it carries something will cannot: that the decision is already made, or that the reason is standing in front of you.
teach.meaning: Going to reaches back before the moment of speaking and picks something up. Sometimes it picks up a decision you took earlier and have been carrying since: nothing is booked, nobody else is involved, but your mind is made up. Sometimes it picks up a piece of the world in front of you, right now, that points at what is coming. Either way the future here has a cause the listener could look at, and that is what separates it from a plain opinion about later.

form.pattern: am / is / are + going to + the plain verb
notes: am with I, is with he, she, it and any single thing, are with you, we and they
in speech it runs together as gonna, but nobody writes that in an essay or a letter
the negative and the question are made on am, is or are, not on going
form.negative: am not / isn't / aren't going to: The depot isn't going to take deliveries on Sunday.
form.question: Am, is or are + person + going to: Are you going to apply for it?

marks.label: the decision was taken, or the sign appeared
and it has been sitting there since

spec.caption: The cause is already behind you. Only the result is still ahead.

worked_example.sentence: The tide is coming in fast, so we're going to lose the causeway.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reason is in front of both people. Anyone standing there can see the water, and the sentence simply reads what the water is saying.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We will lose the causeway would make it a private opinion about the afternoon, as if the speaker had not looked at the water at all.

notice_set.sentence: I'm going to apply for the surveying course in Norland.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker made up their mind before this conversation?
notice_set.why: The decision is already sitting behind the speaker; they are only reporting it now.

notice_set.sentence: Nothing has moved at the barrier for ten minutes, so we're going to be late.
notice_set.question: Can the two people see the reason for saying this?
notice_set.why: The reason is the barrier, and both of them are sitting at it.

notice_set.sentence: Marta is going to hand her notice in at the end of the month.
notice_set.question: Has she agreed a date with anyone yet?
notice_set.why: An intention says her mind is made up. Whether anybody else has been told is simply left out.

notice_set.sentence: Those clouds are going to soak the whole survey team.
notice_set.question: Where is the speaker's reason for saying this?
options: In something they read last week
notice_set.why: The speaker is reading the sky. Take the clouds away and the sentence has nothing left holding it up.

notice_set.sentence: We aren't going to renew the lease on the Marlow unit.
notice_set.question: Is this a plan or a guess?
notice_set.why: It is a decision the speaker's side has already taken, stated as their own.

teach.rule_line: If the cause is already behind you, or in front of you, use going to.
teach.false_rule: That going to is just a longer, more casual will. It carries something will cannot: that the reason for the sentence already exists.

errors.wrong: I think prices are going to fall next year, but nobody really knows.
errors.right: I think prices will fall next year, but nobody really knows.
errors.why_it_happens: Going to gets learned as the everyday future, so it spreads into pure guesswork. The second half of the sentence admits there is no evidence, which is exactly what going to claims there is.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to fall becomes will fall.

errors.wrong: The committee going to review the parking charges in March.
errors.right: The committee is going to review the parking charges in March.
errors.why_it_happens: Going to feels like one solid block of meaning, so the small word in front of it drops off without anybody noticing. It carries no meaning of its own, which is precisely why the ear does not miss it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: is.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of languages that build a sentence without a linking verb.

errors.wrong: Governments are going to have to spend far more on flood defences.
errors.right: Governments will have to spend far more on flood defences.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence is fine English and would pass unremarked in conversation. Written down in a formal argument it sounds like a person talking rather than a case being made.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to have becomes will have.

errors.wrong: Hold on, I'm going to give you a hand with that.
errors.right: Hold on, I'll give you a hand with that.
errors.why_it_happens: The offer is invented in the same breath as the sentence, but going to has become the learner's default, so it turns a spontaneous offer into something the speaker seems to have planned in advance.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: am going to give becomes will give.

pays_in.note: A long turn about a plan is carried almost entirely by it.
pays_in.model: I'm going to move closer to the coast once the lease on the flat runs out.

pays_in.note: Explaining what current signs point to, rather than what you merely believe.
pays_in.model: With rents climbing like that, a lot of younger people are going to leave the city.

pays_in.note: Speakers use it to signal that a decision has already been taken.
pays_in.model: We're going to run the second session in the smaller room instead.

used_in.quote: A card asking about a plan for the next few years is answered in this shape from the first sentence to the last.
Arrangements and intentions are stated aloud in the booking conversation, and the detail sits in the second half of them.

payload.sentence: Devi is going to retrain as a water engineer.
payload.question: Has she made up her mind already?

feedback.why_key: The decision sits behind the sentence. She is not choosing while she speaks; she is telling you what she chose.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask when the decision was taken, not when it happens.

payload.sentence: The river has risen four inches since dawn and the low fields are going to flood.
payload.question: Is the writer guessing, or reading something in front of them?
options: Reading something in front of them

feedback.why_key: The first half of the sentence hands you the reason. Remove it and the second half has nothing standing under it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the reason the writer has already given you.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a company's plans.
payload.sentence: The firm going to open a second workshop in Ashfield.
reasons: a small word is missing in front of going
the plan has not been decided yet
the workshop has already opened
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Going to needs a small word carrying the person and the time in front of it. Without one the sentence never gets started.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that am, is or are is sitting in front of going.

payload.context: Somebody explaining a decision they took last month.
payload.stem: We ___ (sell) the flat and rent something nearer the hospital.

feedback.why_key: The decision was taken before the conversation, so the sentence reaches back and reports it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match am, is or are to the person before you go on.

payload.context: A field note written while the readings are still coming in.
payload.stem: The salinity trace has climbed all morning, so the sensors ___ (need) recalibrating.

feedback.why_key: The trace on the screen is the reason, and it has been visible for hours before the sentence was written.
feedback.feed_forward: Point at the evidence, then choose the shape that admits it.

payload.given: Osman decided last winter. He wants to walk the whole ridge path in one go.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence reporting the decision he is carrying around with him.

expected: is going to walk the whole ridge path in one go
is going to walk the ridge path in one go

feedback.why_key: The choice was made last winter and has not changed since, which is the situation this shape reports.
feedback.feed_forward: Report the old decision, do not make a new one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a plan that has already been announced.

expected: the market is going to close for refurbishment

feedback.why_key: The small word goes in third, before going, and the plain verb waits behind to.
feedback.feed_forward: Build it in order: person, small word, going to, plain verb.

payload.audio_text: We're going to take the coast road instead.

expected: we're going to take the coast road instead
were going to take the coast road instead
we are going to take the coast road instead

feedback.why_key: In real speech the small word collapses onto the person and going to blurs into a single sound. The whole meaning is carried by what you can barely hear.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow the replay and count the sounds before the main verb.

items.decision_cue: are going to have to raise

payload.context: From the closing paragraph of a formal argument about public spending.
payload.sentence: Councils are going to have to raise charges whatever happens to central funding.
reasons: the shape belongs to speech rather than to a formal argument
the councils have not decided anything
the verb behind to is built wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. It simply sounds like somebody talking, and a formal argument wants the flatter word instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Switch to will when the writing is formal.

payload.sentence: The council going to widen the pavements on both sides of the square.

expected: the council is going to widen

feedback.why_key: The plan is real and already taken. The sentence just never says who is doing it or when, because the little word that says so is missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the missing is before going.

items.decision_cue: she has been on her feet since six

payload.context: Two things said about the same nurse at the end of a shift.
sentences: She is going to sleep for twelve hours, she has been on her feet since six.
She will sleep badly again, she always does before an inspection.
meanings: The speaker is working from something they have watched happen all day.
The speaker is working from a pattern they carry in their head.

feedback.why_key: One speaker points at today. The other points at every other time it has happened, which is a different kind of reason altogether.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate what you have seen today from what you generally believe.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one thing you decided months ago to do about your work or studies, which nobody has booked or arranged for you. Say it in one sentence.

feedback.why_key: A decision you have been carrying for months is not made in the sentence, so the sentence has to reach back and pick it up.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a decision you already hold, not a new one.

payload.prompt_text: Speak for one minute on a plan you have for the next few years. Use this shape at least three times, and once let a reason you can actually point to carry the sentence.

feedback.why_key: A long turn about a plan collapses into a list without it, because nothing in the answer says the decisions are already yours.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the plan, then give the reason you can point at.

points.title: Saying what is already in the diary with a time and usually another person

point_json.grammar_name: Present continuous for fixed future arrangements

teach.can_do: I can say what is already arranged for later, with a time attached and usually somebody else expecting me.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the shape English uses for a diary, and learners who do not have it say everything about next week with will, which sounds like nothing has been settled.
teach.meaning: The -ing shape normally says that something is going on around now. Pointed at later, it says something slightly different but very close: the arrangement is going on around now, even though the event itself is not. A time has been picked, a place is usually known, and somebody else is involved and expecting you. That is why it feels solid. You are not saying what you believe or what you have decided alone; you are reading out something that already exists between you and another person.

form.pattern: am / is / are + the -ing verb, with a later time said or understood
notes: the shape is exactly the one you use for things going on around now; the time word is what points it forward
without a later time in the sentence or in the conversation, a listener will hear it as right now
verbs about states rather than doings resist the -ing shape here as much as anywhere else
form.negative: am not / isn't / aren't + the -ing verb: We aren't running the Tuesday session this month.
form.question: Am, is or are + person + the -ing verb: Are you seeing the supervisor on Friday?

left.text: the arrangement, with a time and another person in it

spec.caption: The thing that is going on around now is the arrangement, not the event.

worked_example.sentence: I'm seeing the site manager at four to go through the survey.
worked_example.why_this_form: A time has been agreed and somebody else has it written down too. The speaker is reading out something that already exists between them.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I'll see the site manager at four would sound as if the speaker had just thought of it and the manager knew nothing about it.

notice_set.sentence: Halvard is starting at the Norland office on the ninth.
notice_set.question: Do other people already know about this?
notice_set.why: A date this exact does not exist unless somebody else has agreed to it.

notice_set.sentence: We're taking the last train back on Sunday evening.
notice_set.question: Has a time already been settled?
notice_set.why: The train has a departure time and the speakers have picked it, so the arrangement exists before the sentence does.

notice_set.sentence: Lenka is moving into the flat above the bakery.
notice_set.question: Is this happening at this exact moment, or later?
notice_set.why: The shape is the same for both. What decides it is the time word, or the conversation it sits in.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic isn't taking walk-in patients next Thursday.
notice_set.question: Is this something the clinic has decided in advance?
notice_set.why: A named day tells you the arrangement was made before anyone said this sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Bo and I are meeting the landlord about the damp.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker alone in this?
notice_set.why: Two other people are inside the arrangement, which is the usual situation for this shape.

teach.rule_line: If a time is agreed and somebody else expects you, use the -ing shape.
teach.false_rule: That the -ing shape can only mean right now. Point it at a day next week and it says the day is already fixed.

errors.wrong: I meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.right: I'm meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing verb carries all the meaning, so the small word in front carries none and quietly falls out, especially in speech where it is barely audible in the first place.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: am.

errors.wrong: We are having the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.right: We will have the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Having here means simply possessing, not doing anything, and a verb that describes a state rather than an activity will not go into the -ing shape however firmly the day has been agreed.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are having becomes will have.

errors.wrong: Rents in the city are rising sharply next year.
errors.right: Rents in the city will probably rise sharply next year.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the shape points forward and stops there. Nobody arranges the rent market, so the sentence claims a diary entry that could not exist.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are rising becomes will probably rise.

errors.wrong: Sorry, I can't come, I will help my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.right: Sorry, I can't come, I'm helping my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.why_it_happens: Will is the future the learner reaches for first, so a promise already made to somebody else comes out sounding as if it were being invented on the spot as an excuse.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will help becomes am helping.

pays_in.note: Any question about your week is answered in this shape.
pays_in.model: I'm doing an evening class on Tuesdays until the end of March.

pays_in.note: A letter changing or confirming an arrangement runs on it.
pays_in.model: I'm arriving on the Thursday evening rather than the Friday morning.

pays_in.note: Booking and enrolment conversations state the settled dates this way.
pays_in.model: You're joining the intermediate group, and that one meets on Mondays.

used_in.quote: Telling a friend that the plan has changed means stating what was arranged and what is arranged now, both in this shape.
The enrolment conversation settles a day and a time, and the settled version is announced in exactly this way.

payload.sentence: Nuria is presenting the flood figures at the Tuesday briefing.
payload.question: Does anybody besides Nuria already know about this?

feedback.why_key: A briefing with a day on it has been organised, and organising it took more than one person.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who else would have to know for this to be true.

payload.sentence: The department is closing the library annexe over the summer.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The decision and the dates are in place today. Only the closing itself is still waiting to happen.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate when it was settled from when it happens.

payload.context: Somebody explaining why they cannot make Thursday.
payload.sentence: I seeing the physiotherapist on Thursday morning.
reasons: a small word is missing before the -ing verb
the appointment has not been arranged
Thursday is already over
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing verb cannot stand on its own. Something in front of it has to say who and when.
feedback.feed_forward: Say am, is or are out loud before the -ing verb.

payload.context: Turning down an invitation for the weekend.
payload.stem: I can't, my brother ___ (get) married on the Saturday.

feedback.why_key: A wedding is the most arranged thing there is, so the sentence reads out a date that already exists.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose is, am or are to fit the person in front.

payload.context: From a short message confirming a visit.
payload.stem: Two of us ___ (travel) up on the Wednesday and staying overnight.

feedback.why_key: The message is confirming something already agreed, which is why the writer can name the day without hedging it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the small word to a plural person: are.

payload.given: The ferry booking is confirmed for the eleventh. Two of us are named on it.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence telling a friend what has been arranged for the eleventh.

expected: are taking the ferry on the eleventh

feedback.why_key: A confirmed booking with names on it is the clearest case there is of something already settled between people.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the booking into a sentence about the two of you.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a match that has already been fixed.

expected: we are playing the harbour side on sunday

feedback.why_key: The small word comes second and the -ing verb third, with the agreed day pinned on the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the day at the end and the small word second.

payload.audio_text: She's ringing them back first thing tomorrow.

expected: she's ringing them back first thing tomorrow
shes ringing them back first thing tomorrow
she is ringing them back first thing tomorrow

feedback.why_key: The small word has shrunk to a single hissing sound on the end of she, and that sound is the whole difference between an arrangement and nothing at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of the person word before the -ing verb.

teach.can_do: I can talk about a future set by a timetable, using the same shape I use for things that are generally true.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the smallest of these futures and the one learners skip, so they say the bus will leave at eleven and sound as if they decided it themselves.
teach.meaning: This is the future that belongs to an organisation rather than to a person. A railway, a college, a cinema, a court, a tide table: something outside everybody in the conversation has fixed the clock, published it, and will run to it whether or not anyone in the room turns up. points.title: Choosing which way to point forward, by asking where the future actually lives

point_json.grammar_name: will vs going to vs the -ing shape vs the plain present

teach.can_do: I can pick the right way of pointing forward by asking where the future I am describing actually comes from.
teach.why_it_matters: English has no single future. It has four, and the one you pick tells your listener how settled the situation already is, whether you meant that or not.
teach.meaning: Every sentence about later carries a second message underneath it: how much of this is already real. Say it out of your own head and you are giving an opinion or making up your mind on the spot. Say it with going to and you are pointing back at a decision you already took, or at something in front of you both. Say it with the -ing shape and you are reading out an arrangement another person is expecting you to keep. Say it plainly and you are quoting a printed timetable. Same afternoon, four different claims about how settled it is.

form.pattern: will + plain verb · am/is/are going to + plain verb · am/is/are + -ing verb · the ordinary present shape
notes: all four are ordinary, correct English; nothing here is more advanced than anything else
the choice is about where the future came from, not about how far away it is
an essay prefers will with a softening word for a prediction, and treats going to as speech
form.negative: each of the four goes negative in its own ordinary way; the choice itself does not change.
form.question: Ask yourself the question in the rule line before you open your mouth, not afterwards.

spec.label: how settled is this, and who settled it?

steps.gloss: nobody has settled anything; this is my head, right now
I settled it earlier, or something in front of us points at it
another person settled it with me, and there is a time
an organisation settled it and printed it

notice_set.question: When did the speaker make up their mind?
notice_set.why: Fine is the sound of somebody giving way, which places the decision inside this exchange.

notice_set.why: Nothing in the conversation controls the water. The time is simply printed in a table.

contrast.question: Where does this future live: my head, my plans, our diary, or their timetable?

fork.answer: In my head, right now — I believe it, or I am making up my mind as I speak
In something that already exists — a decision I took earlier, or a sign in front of us
In somebody else's clock — a person expecting me, or a printed timetable if it is an organisation
fork.selects: the -ing shape, or the plain present when nobody in the conversation set the time

a.text: I'll speak to the site manager about the leak.
a.means: The speaker has thought of it this second and is offering to do it.

b.text: I'm speaking to the site manager about the leak.
b.means: It is already arranged, and the manager has it written down too.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose will. That tells your listener the idea has just occurred to you and nobody else knows about it. If the meeting was fixed last week, they will now ask you to arrange it, and you will have to explain twice.

edge_case.text: Shall survives in offers and suggestions, mostly as a question: Shall I carry that? Elsewhere in modern British English will has taken over. Recognise it when you hear it, and do not go looking for places to use it.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask who you would have to tell if you changed your mind. Nobody, because you have only just thought of it, gives you will. Only yourself gives you going to. One named person gives you the -ing shape. Nobody at all, because an organisation owns the time and cannot be argued with, gives you the plain present.

points.title: Keeping will out of the half of the sentence that starts with when, until or as soon as

point_json.grammar_name: Present forms after when, as soon as, before, after, until, once and by the time

teach.can_do: I can join two future events with when, until or as soon as, and put will in only one of them.
teach.why_it_matters: One of the most common errors at this level, and invisible to the person making it, because the broken version sounds perfectly logical in their head.
teach.meaning: Some sentences carry two future events: one is the moment, and the other is what happens at that moment. English marks the future only once. The half that starts with when, until, before, once, after, as soon as or by the time is the moment, and English treats a fixed future moment as though it were already here, so it uses the ordinary present shape. All the pointing forward is done by the other half. Saying it twice does not make the sentence more future; it makes it wrong.

form.pattern: when / before / after / until / once / as soon as / by the time + ordinary present shape ... will + plain verb
notes: the two halves can go in either order; whichever half starts with one of those words keeps the present shape
when the joining half comes first, a comma follows it: Once the results are in, we will decide.
the same words after a verb of knowing or asking are a different job, and there will is normal: nobody knows when it will reopen
form.negative: the joining half goes negative in the ordinary present way: until the road doesn't flood any more.
form.question: What will you do when the contract ends? — the asking half keeps will, the joining half does not.

left.text: when the funding arrives — ordinary present shape, no will

right.text: we will start the second phase — will lives here

spec.caption: One future, marked once. The half with the joining word never gets to carry it.

worked_example.sentence: As soon as the tide drops, the divers will go back down.
worked_example.why_this_form: The dropping tide is the moment the sentence is pointing at, and a moment is treated as fixed. The going down is the news, so that is where the pointing forward happens.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the tide will drop would leave the reader waiting for a main piece of news that never comes, because both halves would be busy announcing the future.

notice_set.sentence: We will move the equipment once the floor dries.
notice_set.question: Has the floor dried yet?
notice_set.why: Both events are still ahead. The drying is simply being treated as the fixed point the moving hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: Ring me when you reach the depot.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about now or about later?
notice_set.why: The arrival has not happened. The sentence borrows the everyday shape for a moment that is still ahead.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody knows when the crossing will reopen.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence about the moment something else happens, or about the reopening itself?
options: About the moment something else happens
notice_set.why: Here the reopening is the whole point of the sentence, not the peg another event hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: By the time the inspectors get here, we will have the paperwork ready.
notice_set.question: Which happens first, in the world?
notice_set.why: By the time sets a deadline, so everything the other half describes has to be done before it.

notice_set.sentence: I won't sign anything until the surveyor sends the report.
notice_set.question: Will the speaker sign if the report never comes?
notice_set.why: Until makes the report the condition, and the sentence says plainly what happens without it.

teach.rule_line: Mark the future once. The half with when, until or as soon as never carries it.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence about the future needs a future word in both halves. English marks it once and lets the joining word do the rest.

errors.wrong: I'll ring you when I will get to the station.
errors.right: I'll ring you when I get to the station.
errors.why_it_happens: Both events are genuinely in the future, so marking both feels honest and complete. Nothing in the sentence sounds odd afterwards, which is why it survives every re-reading.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.
errors.l1_note: Many languages do mark the future in both halves, so this transfers straight across.

errors.wrong: As soon as the figures will arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.right: As soon as the figures arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining half comes first, so the learner starts the sentence in future mode and stays there. By the time the real news arrives, the future has already been announced once.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: We can't begin until the surveyor will arrive on site.
errors.right: We can't begin until the surveyor arrives on site.
errors.why_it_happens: Until feels like a word about waiting, and waiting feels like the future, so the future gets marked again inside the waiting half where it does not belong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: By the time the auditors get here, we finish the whole review.
errors.right: By the time the auditors get here, we will have finished the whole review.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned to strip the future out of the joining half, and strips it out of the other half too. The rule has been over-applied rather than misunderstood.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: will.

the contract has already finished
the two halves are in the wrong order

payload.context: Somebody giving instructions in a kitchen.

ill let you know as soon as i hear back

points.title: Saying what will be going on at a moment later, and asking without pressing

point_json.grammar_name: Future continuous: will be + the -ing verb

teach.can_do: I can say what will already be going on at a particular moment later, and I can ask about someone's plans without sounding as though I want a favour.
teach.why_it_matters: The second job is the one nobody teaches and the one that saves you socially: it lets you ask about somebody's afternoon without them hearing a request coming.
teach.meaning: Pick a moment in the future and stand in it. This shape says that the thing was already under way when you arrived and had not finished. It is the difference between arriving and starting. There is a second job, and in speech it is the more useful one: because the sentence describes a situation rather than a decision, it takes all the pressure out of a question. Asking somebody what they will be doing on Friday enquires about their afternoon. Asking what they will do on Friday sounds like the beginning of a favour.

notes: the small word be never changes and is never dropped, however fast the sentence is said
in speech the whole opening runs together as one blurred sound before the -ing verb
verbs that describe a state rather than an activity stay out of this shape, exactly as they do everywhere else
form.negative: won't be + the -ing verb: The office won't be taking deliveries over the holiday.
form.question: Will + person + be + the -ing verb: Will you be using the van on Thursday?

marks.label: the moment you are talking about

spec.caption: You arrive in the middle of it. It did not start when you got there and it does not stop.

worked_example.sentence: At six on Friday we will still be loading the last of the samples.
worked_example.why_this_form: Six o'clock is a moment the speaker is standing in, and the loading is neither beginning nor ending there. It is simply in progress around it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We will load the last of the samples at six would say the loading begins at six, which is a promise about a start rather than a picture of a moment.

notice_set.sentence: At eleven tomorrow the surveyors will be walking the north boundary.
notice_set.question: Do they begin at eleven?
notice_set.why: Eleven is a moment inside the walk, not the start of it. They set off earlier.

notice_set.sentence: Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for something, or just checking?
notice_set.why: The question describes a situation rather than requesting a decision, so nobody feels pushed by it.

notice_set.sentence: Will you use the meeting room this afternoon?
notice_set.question: Could the listener hear a request coming?
notice_set.why: This one asks the listener to commit, and a commitment question usually has something behind it.

notice_set.sentence: This time next month Kwame will be teaching in Norland.
notice_set.question: Will he have started before that moment?
notice_set.why: The picture is of a job already under way, so the start is somewhere behind the moment named.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic won't be running its evening sessions in August.
notice_set.question: Is this about one evening or about a stretch of weeks?
notice_set.why: The shape stretches an activity out, so August is being described as a whole rather than dated.

teach.rule_line: Stand in a moment later and describe what is already going on around you.
teach.false_rule: That this is just a longer, politer will. It draws a picture of a moment; the politeness is a side effect of describing rather than asking.

errors.wrong: At nine tomorrow we will loading the containers at the north gate.
errors.right: At nine tomorrow we will be loading the containers at the north gate.
errors.why_it_happens: The two small words in the middle carry no meaning of their own and run together in speech, so one of them drops out and the writer's ear does not miss it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: be.

errors.wrong: By this time next year I will be knowing whether the appeal succeeded.
errors.right: By this time next year I will know whether the appeal succeeded.
errors.why_it_happens: Knowing feels like something you do over a long stretch, so the shape that stretches things out looks right. Knowing is a state you are in, not an activity you perform.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: be.

errors.wrong: By Friday afternoon I will be finishing the whole review.
errors.right: By Friday afternoon I will finish the whole review.
errors.why_it_happens: By Friday points at a deadline, which is about getting something done. The shape chosen points at something still in progress, so the sentence promises the opposite of what the writer meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: be.

errors.wrong: Will you drive past the depot on Thursday? I need a favour.
errors.right: Will you be driving past the depot on Thursday? I need a favour.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner asks the direct question because it is shorter, and it lands as a demand for a commitment before the listener has heard what is being asked of them.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: be.

points.title: Standing at a point in the future and saying what is already finished by then

point_json.grammar_name: Future perfect: will have + past participle

teach.can_do: I can pick a point in the future, stand in it, and say what is already over by the time I get there.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shape a projection wants. A chart running to 2040, or an essay forecasting, needs a sentence that looks back from a date nobody has reached.
teach.meaning: Every other way of pointing forward looks at something ahead of you. This one walks past it first. You choose a moment in the future, you stand in it, and from there you look backwards at something that is by then already over. The event itself may be tomorrow or twenty years away; what matters is that it is behind the moment you have chosen. That is why these sentences almost always carry a by: by June, by the time the survey closes, by the end of the decade.

form.pattern: will have + the past participle, which is the shape you already use after have
notes: the past participle is the same word you would use in have finished, have grown, have fallen
in speech will have shrinks to something like will've, and after a pronoun it can vanish almost completely
the sentence nearly always names the future point, usually with by, and it makes very little sense without one
form.negative: won't have + the past participle: The defences won't have failed by then, but they will be close.
form.question: Will + person + have + the past participle: Will the figures have stabilised by March?

marks.label: and is over before you arrive
the moment you stand in and look back from

spec.caption: Walk past the event first. Then turn round and describe it from there.

worked_example.sentence: By 2040 the catchment will have lost around a fifth of its winter rainfall.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence puts the reader in 2040 and looks back over everything that happened on the way there. The loss is not coming; from that vantage point it has already happened.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The catchment will lose a fifth of its rainfall in 2040 would date the loss to that single year, which is a much narrower and much stranger claim.

notice_set.sentence: By the end of March the team will have surveyed every inlet on the coast.
notice_set.question: Is any surveying still going on at the end of March?
notice_set.why: The end of March is the point being looked back from, and the work is behind it.

notice_set.sentence: By the time the report lands, the money will have gone elsewhere.
notice_set.question: Which happens first?
notice_set.why: The looking-back shape always puts its own event behind the moment named.

notice_set.sentence: The gauges won't have failed by the summer, but they will be close to it.
notice_set.question: Are the gauges working in the summer?
notice_set.why: The sentence checks the state of the gauges at the summer and finds them still standing.

notice_set.sentence: Marta will have finished the fieldwork long before the funding runs out.
notice_set.question: Is the fieldwork over when the funding runs out?
notice_set.why: Long before puts a wide gap between the end of the work and the moment being looked back from.

notice_set.sentence: In ten years the town will have grown by half again.
notice_set.question: Is the growth spread over the ten years or squeezed into the last one?
notice_set.why: Looking back from the end of a stretch takes in everything that happened inside it.

teach.rule_line: Choose a moment later, stand in it, and describe what is already behind you.
teach.false_rule: That this is a grander, more academic way of saying will. Use it with no future point named and the sentence has nowhere to look back from.

errors.wrong: By June the team will finished the second phase of the survey.
errors.right: By June the team will have finished the second phase of the survey.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the work is over by June and puts the verb into a finished shape, which feels like enough. The word that does the looking back is the one that carries no meaning of its own, so it is the one that goes missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: have.

errors.wrong: By 2050 the coastal population will have grew by nearly a third.
errors.right: By 2050 the coastal population will have grown by nearly a third.
errors.why_it_happens: Grew is the shape the writer uses far more often, so it arrives first. The shape needed after have is a different one, and for irregular verbs there is nothing in the sentence to remind you.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: grew becomes grown.

errors.wrong: I will have rung the office tomorrow evening about the readings.
errors.right: I will ring the office tomorrow evening about the readings.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape has been learned as the impressive one and gets used to sound more careful. With no later point to look back from, it leaves the reader hunting for a moment the sentence never names.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: have.

errors.wrong: By the time the grant will arrive, the project will have closed.
errors.right: By the time the grant arrives, the project will have closed.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence contains two future events and the writer marks both. The half beginning with by the time is only naming the moment, and a named moment is treated as fixed.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

theyll have signed it off by thursday

feedback.feed_forward: Write the date first, then the finished event.
